messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 45-year-old chef from Oceania, sought help after experiencing persistent distress following a traumatic event. His trauma narrative began with an incident of rape that occurred six months ago. Mark's vivid recollections of the assault were fragmented and confusing. He struggled to put the memories in the right sequence, often feeling as if pieces of his experience were missing or out of order. Mark’s trauma profoundly impacted his sense of self and daily functioning. As a chef, he had always prided himself on his culinary skills and his ability to create dishes that delighted both taste buds and eyes. However, since the assault, he found it increasingly difficult to focus in the kitchen. His hands trembled when he tried to slice vegetables or prepare sauces, and he often felt overwhelmed by the mundane tasks of cooking. Mark had come to believe that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him as a chef. This belief led him to push away memories before they could fully form, preventing him from confronting the traumatic event in its entirety. The fragmented nature of his recollections made it even more challenging for him to process what had happened, reinforcing his feeling of incapability. He felt deeply contaminated by the assault, which only intensified when he thought about certain aspects of the trauma. The sense of dirtiness extended beyond just the physical act; it permeated every aspect of his life. Mark found himself meticulously cleaning and sanitizing everything in his kitchen to a point where this behavior began to interfere with his work. His colleagues noticed that he was increasingly withdrawn and distant, often disappearing into corners for long periods. The contamination feeling also affected how he interacted with others. He became wary of close physical contact, even something as simple as a handshake or a pat on the back from a coworker could make him feel uneasy. Mark’s work environment, which typically thrived on camaraderie and team collaboration, now felt suffocating and oppressive. What frightened Mark most was the realization that his life had been irrevocably altered by this single traumatic event. He began to see himself as permanently damaged, unable to return to the person he once was. This belief further exacerbated his memory issues; every time he tried to fully confront the memories of what happened, he pushed them away due to the overwhelming sense that these memories confirmed his inability to cope. The negative appraisals about his capabilities and life trajectory had a cyclical effect on his ability to remember and process the trauma. As Mark became more convinced that his life was destroyed by the event, he found it increasingly difficult to integrate and order the fragmented pieces of memory. This cycle intensified over time, leading him to isolate himself both at work and in his personal life. The combination of these factors culminated in a significant decline in Mark’s professional performance and social relationships. His colleagues noted that his dishes lacked their usual creativity and flair, and he had become withdrawn from family gatherings with his children. Finally, the mounting pressure from his employer to improve his performance, coupled with an acute episode where he broke down while working late at the restaurant, pushed Mark to seek help. He was most afraid of never regaining a sense of normalcy or control over his life but also held hope that therapy could provide him with tools to navigate and overcome these overwhelming feelings. Mark’s current state reflects a profound struggle with the aftermath of trauma, where his negative appraisals about himself and life have become deeply intertwined with his memory issues. He seeks help not just to alleviate symptoms, but to reclaim aspects of his identity and regain control over his life.
